doc.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012

title: Playing with Calvin Jackson, Basin Street, meeting Armstrong, and Goodman's visit
summary: He joined pianist Calvin Jackson's quartet, played Basin Street and the Roundtable, met Louis Armstrong, and noticed Goodman in the audience.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: You’re the first person I told this story to I think. So I didn’t get it, and I’m glad I didn’t. Because it would take me away again, and I was concentrating on getting my own thing going eventually. I got a job with a man called Calvin Jackson. He was a brilliant pianist. He was the assistant musical director at MGM with Johnny Green. Brilliant musician. And he had this job, at a very nice sophisticated hotel in Toronto, and a weekly radio series and a weekly television series. And he hired me to be a guest on the television series. He liked me so much he asked me to join the quartet, which I did, and I went with him for about a year or so, and we played all the eastern seaboard — Chicago, Cleveland, we went to New York — and as a matter of fact we were opposite Ella and Oscar in New York at the Basin Street, which was a good experience. It was run by a very, very nice man called Ralph Watkins. And some years later, after I left Calvin, he hired me to play the Embers in New York, and then Morris Levy asked me to do 15 weeks a year with my own group at the Roundtable in New York. And I remember going back to see Ralph Watkins because he had Basin Street, and Pops, Louis Armstrong, was there. And he said, “Have you ever met Mr. Armstrong?” I said, “No, I’d love to meet him.” “Oh,” he said, “come on, we’ll take you to the dressing room.” So he took me to the dressing room and he opened the door, and here’s Pops sitting there, he had just a pair of jockey shorts on, and he had a handkerchief on his head with each corner tied with a little knot, you know. And oh he was so nice to me and so encouraging. So that was a great experience, meeting him, and then of course at the Roundtable I worked opposite people like Andre Previn and all these major stars, and it was great. So I really did enjoy it. It was a great period in my life. And I still did a bit of traveling. And then one night I looked down and here’s Benny Goodman in the audience. And so I naturally played all the Goodman stuff, you know. So I went down afterwards and said, “Good evening, Mr. Goodman, I hope you’re having a nice time.” Anyway, that was about it. And so we went back, and twelve years later, twelve years — now Benny had a reputation of having a bad memory. He called everybody Pops, even his wife. But I can tell you for a fact he didn’t have a bad memory, and I’ll explain that to you in a moment. Anyway, twelve years later he came back to Toronto with Derek Smith to play a concert for the CBC Big Band, Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. And it was a great concert.
